title: Piano Concerto No. 2 in F major
hook: A birthday present from father to son, with a joke about piano practice in the finale.

painting.title: Two Young Girls at the Piano
painting.collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
painting.pairingNote: Two girls practising at the piano at home: the everyday scales and exercises that Shostakovich, writing for his son Maxim, turned into a game.

facts: Shostakovich wrote the concerto in early 1957 for his son Maxim, a piano student at the Moscow Conservatory. Maxim gave the first performance on 10 May 1957, his nineteenth birthday, at his graduation concert.
It was written to be playable by a gifted young pianist, like his earlier Concertino for two pianos. Cheerful music is rare in Shostakovich, and this is among his sunniest works.

He was dismissive of it. A week after finishing it he wrote to a younger composer that it had “no redeeming artistic merits”. Writers have suggested that, after years of official criticism, he was getting his own disparagement in first.
Listeners disagreed with him from the start. It is one of his most popular pieces, and its first movement became the animated tale of *The Steadfast Tin Soldier* in Disney’s *Fantasia 2000* (1999).
The orchestra has no trumpets or trombones: woodwind, four horns, timpani, snare drum and strings.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a perky march (I), a quiet, tender song (II), a dance with a joke about piano exercises (III).

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: A bright, busy [[sonata-form|sonata form]] that begins with a bassoon and builds to a march. The piano’s first tune is simple enough for a beginner, both hands an octave apart, but the movement grows more brilliant as it goes, with a solo [[cadenza|cadenza]] in which the piano plays several voices at once.

mainIdeas.name: The bassoon tune
mainIdeas.description: perky and marching, the orchestra’s theme.

mainIdeas.name: The piano tune
mainIdeas.description: a plain, quick line played in octaves, which turns into a march.

mainIdeas.name: The D minor tune
mainIdeas.description: darker, in bare octaves on the piano.

stops.hear: A bassoon alone plays a perky little tune; clarinets and oboes join in
The piano enters with its own quick tune, both hands an octave apart
stops.happening: The piano’s theme, in F major

stops.hear: The tune turns into a brisk march, piano and orchestra together
Darker: the piano plays a new tune in bare octaves, which winds down to almost nothing
stops.happening: A second theme, in D minor

stops.hear: A sudden blast from the orchestra; the piano pounds out low, jumping octaves while the orchestra roars the piano’s first tune
The whole orchestra blazes out the D minor tune, now broad and triumphant in B-flat major
The piano alone, one voice entering after another
stops.happening: A solo [[cadenza|cadenza]] that begins as a [[fugato|fugato]]

stops.hear: The orchestra returns with the melody high in the woodwind; the piano runs up and down in scales

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: The opening tune resurfaces and the movement snaps shut

notice: Listen to the piano’s first entry. Both hands play the same notes an octave apart: the kind of thing a student practises, made to sound like real music.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Leonard Bernstein plays the piano and conducts the New York Philharmonic, recorded in January 1958, less than a year after the Moscow premiere. On the Spotify album the concerto is tracks 5–7, after the First Piano Concerto with André Previn at the piano.

movements.heading: Andante
movements.summary: The heart of the concerto: a slow, tender song. The strings begin alone in C minor; the piano enters in a gentle C major with a melody whose accompaniment moves in threes against the strings’ twos. The movement does not end but flows straight into the finale.

mainIdeas.name: The string introduction
mainIdeas.description: slow, hushed and a little sad.

mainIdeas.name: The piano’s song
mainIdeas.description: a simple, songlike melody, calm and unhurried.

stops.hear: The strings alone, slow and hushed
The piano enters softly with a simple, tender melody
stops.happening: The piano’s theme, in C major

stops.hear: The strings take up the melody; the piano accompanies with quiet, rippling notes
stops.happening: The theme passed to the orchestra

stops.hear: The piano’s melody grows fuller, in rich chords, then subsides
The strings’ opening music returns, with the piano’s line floating above

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: Very quiet; the music does not close but slides straight into the next movement

notice: Listen to the piano’s accompaniment against the strings: three notes in the piano for every two in the orchestra. It gives the music its gentle, rocking feel.

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: A dance in two beats that dashes along on folk-like five-note scales, with a second tune in a lopsided seven-beat metre. In between, the piano breaks into rattling scale exercises, the joke for a graduating piano student.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a fast, bright tune built on the [[pentatonic-scale|pentatonic scale]].

mainIdeas.name: The seven-beat tune
mainIdeas.description: lopsided and swinging, with plucked strings like balalaikas.

mainIdeas.name: The exercise
mainIdeas.description: scales in parallel, the kind pianists practise from the Hanon exercise book.

stops.hear: The piano races off in a bright, fast dance, the orchestra snapping at its heels
stops.happening: The first theme, in F major

stops.hear: A lopsided tune in seven beats, the strings plucking like balalaikas
stops.happening: The second theme, in 7/8, with [[pizzicato|pizzicato]] strings

stops.hear: The piano rattles up and down in parallel scales, like a practice exercise
stops.happening: The “Hanon” theme: the joke for Maxim

stops.hear: The three ideas jostle, combine and chase each other
The seven-beat tune once more

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: A brilliant dash in F major

notice: Count the beats when the plucked-string tune arrives: seven to a bar, grouped unevenly, which is why it limps so cheerfully.

threads.title: Father and son
threads.body: Written for Maxim’s graduation and birthday, the concerto is pitched for a young player: clear textures, octaves, scales.

threads.title: Exercises into music
threads.body: Octaves in the first movement, rocking threes in the second and Hanon scales in the third: the stuff of piano practice turned into tunes.

threads.title: Lightness
threads.body: No trumpets, no trombones and few clouds: a rare holiday in Shostakovich’s music.
